PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — below are the further questions we have sent to the planning department.
text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — below are the further questions we have sent to the planning department.

15. There are lots of steps. How will the elevated levels be accessible for wheelchairs, mobility aids, prams etc?

16. Will local Fire Rescue Victoria teams need additional specialised equipment for the proposed tall buildings?

17. To what degree are the car parks ‘adaptive’, insofar as they could be turned into apartments, and under what circumstances would that happen?

18. How will rebuilding East Block with a structure above it meet heritage requirements? Could the design better preserve its heritage and identity?

19. For stage 2, the plans state: “Gas requirement for market expansion to be developed”. The ESD report says no new gas. Will there be any new gas connections across any stage?

20. When will the Green Travel Plan and public/active transport assessments be completed?

21. What will be the mix of apartments?

22. There is a risk of rat-running through the north-south streets, especially during peak hour. How will that be addressed?

23. Does Earle Street really need vehicle traffic?

24. What are the plans for the vacant government-owned land on the corner of Murray Rd and St Georges Rd? Can that site be used to provide parking in the first instance and more social or affordable housing in the long term?

25. Will every existing trader who wants to remain at Preston Market be able to return after redevelopment? How many traders will need to temporarily relocate during construction? What support will they receive?

26. What legal mechanism will guarantee that the privately owned public open spaces (including the elevated open spaces) remain publicly accessible in perpetuity?

27. How much direct sunlight will the existing market receive in winter compared with today?

28. Of the 811 car spaces associated with the market, how many will be available at each stage, and are these spaces shared with the supermarkets and other retail uses?

29. Will there be an in-house car sharing program for residents?

(For the first 14 questions, see our earlier post. We’re hoping to receive answers to the first batch tomorrow.)

Talking about the oval!
text:
Talking about the oval!

For reasons we don’t fully understand, approximately 20,000 cubic metres of soil was dumped on the William Ruthven ovals between 2013 and 2015 (though there may have already been earlier fill on the site).

Reports describe the soil as “uncontrolled fill”, meaning there is no documented engineering control over how it was placed or compacted. The soil is also predominantly clay. It was not ever likely to create a good sporting surface.

If anyone has any further information, please let us know.

Unfortunately, fixing the problem will require significant and costly earthworks.

-- with Premier @[100058101160143:2048:Ben Carroll MP] at @[100063581503427:2048:William Ruthven Secondary College]

Merrilands Uniting Early Learning will cease providing long day care from 2027. Below is a summary of what we
text:
Merrilands Uniting Early Learning will cease providing long day care from 2027. Below is a summary of what we know about the issue.

— Approximately 38 families will be affected.

— Uniting says “the centre has been struggling to attract families for the last four to five years” and believes this is linked to “an increase in new childcare centres nearby”.

— However, families have reported that it has been difficult to obtain daycare places.

— Furthermore, it is not clear why a well-regarded, long-standing local centre would lose daycare enrolments to newer centres with typically higher fees.

— The Department of Education and Darebin Council are working to assist families to find alternative long day care.

— @[100064262696580:2048:Uniting Vic.Tas] has been running childcare at the centre since 1985.

— The centre is covered by VECTEA (the Victorian Early Childhood Teachers and Educators Agreement).

We are seeking further information regarding the decision.

title: VISY UPDATE – if you are concerned about the odours from the Visy recycling plant, please sign the parliamenta
text:
VISY UPDATE – if you are concerned about the odours from the Visy recycling plant, please sign the parliamentary petition via the link in the comments. 

BACKGROUND INFO

Visy has been producing cardboard packaging at the Radford Road site since 1959. The recycling plant opened in 1983.

There is some debate about when the odour issue started. Many people date it to roughly 2020, when Visy began recycling more water and using more household feedstock (which includes more food residue than industrial feedstock).

Bacteria in the plant’s recycled water systems produced sulphides and volatile fatty acids, which can cause strong odours.

Following complaints from residents, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) issued a series of notices to Visy requiring the company to investigate and rectify the issue. The rectification measures included:

— introducing a bacteria control program (from 2020)
— increasing the use of fresh water for flushing (from 2021)
— switching back to industrial feedstock (from 2022)
— sealing roof vents and building gaps (2022–2025)
— extending exhaust systems and installing new stacks and fans (2021–2026).

Visy claims that the changes have resulted in a 91% reduction in measured odour units at the plant.

However, we don’t believe the reduction experienced in the community has been anywhere near that amount.

We have doorknocked all homes within 500 metres of the plant: once in 2022 and again this year.

While different people have different senses of smell, the odours remain a serious problem for many households. In 2022, we estimated that more than 200 households felt the odours were having a major negative impact on their lives. In 2026, we estimate that more than 100 households continue to be affected that way.

A local resident, Frieda De Doncker, has started a petition asking the EPA to impose further, urgent odour control requirements. We support that ask.

We are sponsoring the petition to provide further evidence about the number of households affected.

We will continue to raise the issue in parliament and with the minister.

ERIC STREET UPDATE — the two public housing walk-ups at 15–17 Eric Street have been proposed for demolition.
text:
ERIC STREET UPDATE — the two public housing walk-ups at 15–17 Eric Street have been proposed for demolition.

In the reel, I say that the Minister for Planning has given permission for demolition to proceed. To be completely accurate, a final decision hasn’t been made yet. Homes Victoria has completed the consultation and is preparing a planning application for demolition. If you have any questions or concerns, we can still follow up.

Some other points of note from reading the reports…

— The planning report says the vacant apartments are no longer suitable for housing due to their age, poor condition, fire damage, poor environmental performance and the difficulty of bringing them up to current building standards.

— The heritage report says the statement of significance in the original heritage overlay was not accurate in describing the blocks as “an unusual development of pre-cast concrete walk-up flats”. Nonetheless, it recommends the preparation of an archival-quality photographic record in accordance with Heritage Victoria’s guidelines.

— The preliminary arboricultural report assesses 24 trees within the site itself. It says the concept design may allow some trees in the central courtyard to be retained, including two mature melaleucas. Most trees on the site are exotics.

title: Most linear reserves in Preston and Reservoir have water pipes or underground creeks beneath them.
text:
Most linear reserves in Preston and Reservoir have water pipes or underground creeks beneath them.

This is often used as a reason why walking paths or vegetation cannot be added, even though other parts of Melbourne have paths and planting over similar infrastructure.

We have asked the Minister for Water about developing a more consistent approach so local reserves can be better used by the community.

Relevant local reserves include:

— Northern Pipe Trail (@[100064863125422:2048:Melbourne Water] pipes),
— Regent Linear Reserve (Melbourne Water and @[100064783356076:2048:Yarra Valley Water] pipes),
— Maroondah Aqueduct Linear Reserve (Melbourne Water pipes),
— Ruthven Linear Reserve (underground creek),
— Elsey Road Linear Reserve (underground creek),
— Union Reserve (underground creek) and
— Camera Walk near the Coburg Hill shops (Melbourne Water pipes).

text:
The Northern Panthers have been part of Reservoir since 1977, bringing together kids from diverse backgrounds to enjoy rugby — including future stars Christian Leali’ifano, Rob Leota, Josh Coward, Junior Laloifi, Tegan French and Silei Poluleuligaga.

Thanks to club president Grant Wason and secretary Jo Tevaga for all the work they do to support the players and families, and for chatting to us about their plans for improved lighting at CH Sullivan Memorial Reserve to support the continued development of women’s and girls’ rugby.

— with Grant Wason and @[100063848375357:2048:Mayor Emily Dimitriadis] at @[100063508001179:2048:Northern Panthers Rugby Union Club]

UPDATE: some more historical information from the club, for those interested... The club played its first season in 1977 at Donath Reserve. The ground was on the eastern side of Cheddar Road, now occupied by Keon Park FC. The basketball stadium acted as the club rooms, though the Junction Hotel was the unofficial club room. The Club was formed in 1976, and fielded a team in a sevens tournament, which they won. The following year was the first full fifteen-a-side competitive team entry. So next year will mark fifty years of competition.

PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the s
text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the sale of the Tarascio family’s component to their joint venture partners, the Medich family, in August last year.

Any such development would take years to plan — and years to build, across multiple stages.

However, if anyone is interested, there is a large amount of information online about what state government planning provisions would apply. Some of the key requirements are:

— ensure the market buildings with heritage significance are substantially retained, including the large murals, and maintain a working market with a minimum floor area of 12,700 m^2 

— provide approx 1,200 dwellings, including social and affordable housing, with a discretionary maximum of 14 storeys at the northern end and 4 storeys at the southern end 

— include approx 27,500 m^2 of retail floor space, and 5,000 m^2 of office floor space 

— provide a public open space adjacent to the market with a minimum area of 2,700 m^2 and a public open space adjacent to Preston Station of approx 1,000 m^2, with the ownership of both to be transferred to Darebin Council 

— encourage a modal shift to active and public transport 

— ensure adequate car parking for the market and other uses

— encourage loading, servicing and car parking areas to be located underground 

— encourage best-practice environmentally sustainable development outcomes in line with statewide commitments to net zero emissions, and achieve an average 0.5 stars above the prevailing NatHERS requirement for each building 

— provide electric charging points for bicycles and cars 

— provide for the use of alternatives to gas 

— deliver appropriate development staging to allow continuity of market trade throughout the redevelopment of the precinct and to support the viability of business for stall holders.

Note that if any development did proceed, it would probably begin on the two sites west of the train line at St Georges/Murray and St Georges/Cramer. They have maximum heights of 13 and 8 storeys respectively.

text:

title: Thanks to @[100046768729519:2048:Ged Kearney] for organising today’s community safety forum at Preston Library
text:
Thanks to @[100046768729519:2048:Ged Kearney] for organising today’s community safety forum at Preston Library.

Issues discussed included:

— police resourcing, including resourcing for family violence and gendered violence
— the Northland incidents and changes to Northland security
— combatting far-right extremism
— anti-vilification changes
— bail changes
— the role of CCTV footage and the importance of police securing footage promptly
— early intervention programs, including local Darebin programs and the Youth Crime Prevention Program
— technological changes in car theft
— the importance of police providing feedback on incident reports and on Professional Standards Command complaints
— police oversight bodies
— gambling reform and its relationship to family violence
— the difficulty of getting police to pursue criminal allegations related to civil building disputes
— online crime (and resources provided by Bridge Darebin), and
— the recent Thorne Harbour / Ged Kearney discussion about LGBTQIA+ experiences of family, domestic and sexual violence.

Thanks to everyone who joined Ged’s forum including @[100057983683033:2048:Kat Theophanous MP], @[61556739886183:2048:Mayor Kristine Olaris OAM], Darebin CEO Anne Howard, @[100064780360735:2048:Bridge Darebin] CEO Chris Lombardo and Acting Inspector Michael Pope from Victoria Police.

Reservoir is a very big suburb, and people sometimes ask, “Is it Melbourne’s biggest?”.

title: Over the last two weeks, I’ve received hundreds of emails and messages about the events in Israel, Gaza and th
text:
Over the last two weeks, I’ve received hundreds of emails and messages about the events in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. 

We have all been horrified by the suffering and loss.

Many government MPs spoke about the issue in parliament this week. Our contributions reflected our different perspectives, but we were united in our belief that the priority for the Victorian Government must be our own multicultural communities.

Thousands of Palestinian and Jewish Victorians have friends or family caught up in the conflict. Many are fearful and anxious. Social media content can compound their anxiety. One-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Palestinian suffering circulate in our Muslim communities, and one-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Israeli suffering circulate in our Jewish communities.

The priority for the Victorian Labor Government, as the Premier has made clear, is to provide love and support to all Victorians who have friends or family in Israel, Gaza or the West Bank, regardless of their religion or race. The last two weeks have been incredibly tragic for some, and traumatic for most. People who have spent their lives hoping for peace have seen it ripped away again.

We have spoken with affected local residents. Our thoughts are with them. We will provide any support we can during this time of worry, suffering and grief.

title: Today, we tabled the @[100071960739450:2048:Save the Preston Market] petition. Some of the signatures were fro
text:
Today, we tabled the @[100071960739450:2048:Save the Preston Market] petition. Some of the signatures were from last year, and some things have changed since then, but the general message of the petition hasn't.
 
The petition had 4,693 valid signatures (ie, handwritten signatures accompanied by a full name and full address). That makes it the largest petition tabled in parliament in the last three years.

(UPDATE: as per the comments below, I should clarify that in addition to the 4,963 valid signatures there were also approximately 1,928 handwritten signatures that didn't include their full details and 4,815 typed signatures for a total of 11,490 signatures across over 1,500 pages. It was a very big petition!)

(Also thanks to Jake who was doing work experience for helping count them all, if that's not a classic work experience task I don't know what is 😊)

text: Yesterday, I gave my inaugural speech to parliament. As per tradition, I took the chance to thank my friends, family and loved ones (including my now-fiancée, Noah!). But I also highlighted some of the issues people have raised across Preston and Reservoir, and some of the policies we’re prioritising.
